items.title: Study Strategy
items.text:

items.title: Topic 1: OS Introduction & Computer System Organization
items.text: Source: Lecture 1 + Textbook Ch. 1 (Silberschatz Ch. 1-2, Stallings Ch. 1-2, Stevens & Rago Ch. 1)

items.title: 1.1 What is an Operating System?
items.text:
Definition (Silberschatz): "An operating system is a program that acts as an intermediary between a user of a computer and the computer hardware."

Two Views: | View | Role | |------|------| | User View | Convenience, ease of use, performance | | System View | Resource Allocator (CPU, memory, I/O) + Control Program (prevent errors, control I/O) |

Kernel: "The one program running at all times on the computer" — everything else is system programs or applications.

items.title: 1.2 Computer System Organization (4 Components)
items.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Users                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│    Application Programs             │  ← Compilers, browsers, DBs, games
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│         Operating System            │  ← Resource allocator + control
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│           Hardware                  │  ← CPU, Memory, I/O Devices
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

Hardware Components: - CPU(s): General-purpose + special-purpose (GPU, disk controller, NIC) - Memory: RAM (volatile), ROM/EEPROM (firmware) - I/O Devices: Disk, keyboard, mouse, network, display - System Bus: Connects CPU, memory, device controllers - Memory Controller: Synchronizes access to shared memory

items.title: 1.3 System Boot Process
items.text: Step Description 1. Power On / Reset CPU PC → firmware address (ROM/EEPROM) 2. Bootstrap Program First code to run; initializes CPU, devices, memory; locates & loads kernel 3. Kernel Initialization Sets up system services, interrupt vectors, starts init process 4. Init Process First user process (init or systemd, PID 1); waits for login/daemons

items.title: 1.4 Interrupt-Driven Operation
items.text: Modern OS is interrupt-driven — sits idle waiting for events.

items.title: Interrupt Classification
items.text:
Interrupt Event
    ├── Hardware Interrupt
    │     ├── Polling (CPU queries devices)
    │     └── Vectored (hardware provides offset → Interrupt Vector Table → ISR)
    └── Software Interrupt (Trap/Exception)
          ├── Error (divide by zero, invalid memory access → SIGSEGV)
          └── System Call (user requests OS service)

items.title: Interrupt Handling Lifecycle
items.text:
1. Generation — IRQ from device or trap instruction
  2. Processor Response — Halts current thread at instruction boundary
  3. State Preservation — Saves PC, PSW, registers to kernel stack
  4. Dispatching — Vectored (via IVT) or Polling
  5. Handler Execution — ISR runs (e.g., read keyboard buffer)
  6. State Restoration — Restore registers/PC, resume interrupted thread

Key Insight: Interrupts enable multiprogramming — CPU switches to another process while I/O completes.

items.title: 1.5 Storage Hierarchy
items.text: Level Technology Speed Capacity Volatility Cost/Byte Registers CPU internal Fastest Smallest Volatile Highest Cache (L1/L2/L3) SRAM Very Fast Small Volatile High Main Memory (RAM) DRAM Fast Medium Volatile Medium SSD / NVRAM Flash Fast Large Non-volatile Medium Hard Disk (HDD) Magnetic Slow Very Large Non-volatile Low Tape / Optical Magnetic/Optical Slowest Huge Non-volatile Lowest

items.title: Caching Principle
items.text:
1. Copy data from slower → faster storage temporarily
  2. Cache Hit → read from fast cache
  3. Cache Miss → fetch from slow storage, populate cache
  4. Replacement policies: LRU, FIFO, etc.

items.title: DMA (Direct Memory Access)
items.text:
• Problem: Interrupt per byte wastes CPU for high-speed devices
  • Solution: DMA controller transfers blocks directly between device buffer ↔ memory
  • Result: Only one interrupt per block; CPU executes user code concurrently

items.title: I/O Modes
items.text: Mode Behavior Synchronous (Blocking) CPU waits for I/O completion; one request at a time Asynchronous (Non-blocking) CPU continues immediately; checks completion later

items.title: 1.7 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. OS = Resource Allocator + Control Program (Silberschatz §1.2.1)
  2. Kernel = the one program running at all times (Silberschatz §1.2.1)
  3. Interrupts = OS's nervous system (Silberschatz §1.5)
  4. Storage hierarchy trades speed vs capacity vs cost (Silberschatz §1.4)
  5. DMA offloads bulk data movement from CPU (Silberschatz §1.7.3)
  6. Boot: Firmware → Bootstrap → Kernel → Init (PID 1)

items.title: 1.8 Quick Self-Test
items.text: Question Answer What are the two main roles of an OS from system view? Resource Allocator + Control Program What is the kernel? The one program running at all times How does vectored interrupt differ from polling? Hardware provides offset into IVT; polling = CPU queries each device What happens during DMA transfer? Device ↔ memory directly; 1 interrupt/block; CPU free Why is storage organized hierarchically? Trade-off: speed ↑, cost ↑, capacity ↓, volatility ↑ as you go up

items.title: Topic 2: Computer Architecture & OS Operations
items.text: Source: Lecture 2 + Textbook Ch. 2 (Silberschatz Ch. 1-2, Stallings Ch. 2, 15, Stevens & Rago Ch. 2)

items.title: Single Processor Systems
items.text:
• One general-purpose CPU
  • Special-purpose processors: disk controller, keyboard controller, GPU
  • Run limited instruction sets; offload main CPU (e.g., disk controller handles scheduling)

items.title: Characteristics
items.text:
• Two or more processors in close communication
  • Share: system bus, clock, memory, peripheral devices

items.title: Three Advantages
items.text: Advantage Description Increased Throughput More work in less time (not N× due to sync overhead) Economy of Scale Share peripherals, storage, power — cheaper than N single-CPU systems Fault Tolerance Failure of one CPU ≠ system halt; graceful degradation

items.title: Asymmetric Multiprocessing (AMP)
items.text:
Master CPU → Controls system, schedules, allocates work
Worker CPUs → Execute assigned tasks only
- Simple but master becomes bottleneck

items.title: Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP) — Modern Standard
items.text:
All CPUs are PEERS — no master-slave
Each runs kernel + user code
Each has private registers + cache
All share physical memory via system bus
- Used by: Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS

SMP Architecture:
  CPU 0          CPU 1          CPU 2
  [Regs] [Cache] [Regs] [Cache] [Regs] [Cache]
     │             │             │
     └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                   ▼
            System Bus
                   │
                   ▼
           Shared Memory

items.title: 2.4 Multicore Design
items.text:
• Multiple computing cores on single chip
  • Each core = independent physical CPU to OS
  • Benefits: Faster on-chip communication, less power/heat than multi-chip
Dual-Core Chip:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │         PROCESSOR CHIP          │
  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐     │
  │  │  CORE 0  │  │  CORE 1  │     │
  │  │ [Regs]   │  │ [Regs]   │     │
  │  │ [L1]     │  │ [L1]     │     │
  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘     │
  │       │             │           │
  │       └──────┬──────┘           │
  │              ▼                  │
  │       [Shared L2/L3 Cache]      │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                 │
           Main Memory

# Check your CPU topology
cat /proc/cpuinfo | more

items.title: 2.5 Advanced Architectures
items.text: Architecture Description Blade Servers High-density: multiple processor/I/O boards in one chassis; each boots independently Clustered Systems Independent nodes + shared SAN; Asymmetric (hot-standby) / Symmetric (all active) / HPC (MPI/OpenMP) NUMA Non-Uniform Memory Access — latency varies by CPU-memory distance; scheduler must consider locality big.LITTLE Heterogeneous cores (performance + efficiency); scheduler migrates tasks based on workload

items.title: Dual-Mode Operation
items.text:
• User Mode (bit = 1): Applications run; restricted instructions
  • Kernel Mode (bit = 0): OS runs; privileged instructions allowed
USER MODE (bit=1)                 KERNEL MODE (bit=0)
+-----------------------------+   +-----------------------------+
| User Process executing      |   |                             |
|                             |   |                             |
| Calls system call           |   |                             |
| (e.g. read())               |   |                             |
|         │                   |   |                             |
|         v                   |   |                             |
|   [ TRAP / SYSCALL ] ------>|-->| System call handled         |
|   (HW sets bit = 0)         |   | Execute privileged routine  |
|                             |   |         │                   |
|                             |<--|<--------|--- [ RETURN ]     |
| Resume user execution <-----+   |     (HW resets bit = 1)    |
+-----------------------------+   +-----------------------------+

items.title: Transition Lifecycle
items.text:
1. User program executes in user mode (bit = 1)
  2. Program needs OS service → executes system call (trap instruction)
  3. Hardware: traps, saves CPU state, switches mode bit to 0 (kernel mode)
  4. Kernel: looks up syscall table, verifies parameters, executes privileged function
  5. Kernel: executes return-from-trap (privileged instruction)
  6. Hardware: restores state, sets mode bit to 1 (user mode)
  7. Control returns to user process

items.title: Privileged Instructions (Kernel Mode Only)
items.text:
• Direct I/O manipulation
  • Clearing interrupts
  • Setting timer counters
  • Modifying page tables
  • Context switching

items.title: 2.7 Timer & CPU Protection
items.text:
Purpose: Prevent user programs from hogging CPU (infinite loops)

Mechanism:
1. Hardware timer set to interrupt after interval (fixed or variable)
2. Variable timers: fixed-rate clock + internal counter
3. OS loads initial counter via PRIVILEGED INSTRUCTION before dispatch
4. Each clock tick: counter decrements
5. Counter reaches 0 → hardware timer interrupt
6. Interrupt → OS scheduler → preempt current process → assign CPU to another

items.title: 2.8 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. SMP = peer CPUs sharing memory; standard for modern OS (Silberschatz §2.1.2)
  2. Multicore = multiple cores on one die; each appears as CPU to OS (Silberschatz §2.2)
  3. Clusters = independent nodes + shared SAN; for HA and HPC (Silberschatz §2.3.2)
  4. NUMA/big.LITTLE = modern complexities OS scheduler must handle (Silberschatz §2.3.3-4)
  5. Dual-mode: mode bit in PSW; hardware enforces privileged instruction restriction
  6. System call = trap instruction → mode switch → kernel handler → return
  7. Timer = hardware mechanism enabling preemptive scheduling

items.title: 2.9 Quick Self-Test
items.text: Question Answer AMP vs SMP — which is modern standard? SMP (all CPUs peers) In SMP, what do CPUs share? System bus, clock, memory, peripherals What does each core in multicore have? Private registers + L1 cache What do cores share on-chip? L2/L3 cache What prevents user program from executing privileged instruction? Hardware checks mode bit; traps if user mode (bit=1) How does timer enable preemption? Counter decrements each tick; at 0 → interrupt → scheduler runs

items.title: 2.10 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q4: Special-purpose processors (disk controller, GPU) offload main CPU
  • Q5: Multiprocessor advantages — throughput, economy of scale, fault tolerance (graceful degradation)
  • Q6-7: AMP (master-worker) vs SMP (peers) — know the diagram
  • Q8: Multicore benefits — faster on-chip comm, less power/heat
  • Q9: Blade servers — high-density, each boots independently
  • Q10-11: Clustered systems — SAN, DLM, asymmetric vs symmetric clustering
  • Q12: Multiprogramming — CPU always has job; when one waits for I/O, switch to another
  • Q13: Multitasking/time-sharing — logical extension, rapid response (<1 sec), needs virtual memory
  • Q14: Interrupt-driven — hardware interrupt (devices) vs software interrupt (trap/exception/syscall)
  • Q15-16: Dual-mode — mode bit (0=kernel, 1=user), transition via trap/syscall
  • Q17: Timer — prevents infinite loops, enables preemption, loaded via privileged instruction

items.title: Topic 3: OS Services, System Calls & Process Concept
items.text: Source: Lecture 3 + Textbook Ch. 3 (Silberschatz Ch. 2-3, Stallings Ch. 3-4, Stevens & Rago Ch. 3, 7-8)

items.title: Services Helpful to Users
items.text: Service Description User Interface CLI (shells), GUI (windows), Batch (scripts) Program Execution Load, schedule, allocate, handle termination I/O Operations Safe abstracted access to devices File System Create/delete/read/write, permissions, metadata Communications Shared memory, message passing, pipes, sockets Error Detection Hardware errors, I/O errors, program errors (overflow, segfault)

items.title: Services for System Efficiency
items.text: Service Description Resource Allocation CPU, memory, disk, I/O — fair & efficient Accounting Track usage per user/process (billing, capacity planning) Protection & Security Controlled access, authentication, isolation, defense

items.title: 3.2 System Calls
items.text: Definition: Programmatic interface to kernel services; written in C/assembly; exposed via APIs.

items.title: Example: File Copy Sequence (Silberschatz Fig 2.2)
items.text:
1. Acquire input file name:
   write() → display prompt
   read()  → accept keyboard input

2. Acquire output file name:
   write() → display prompt
   read()  → accept keyboard input

3. Open input file:
   open()  → if not exist, abort & print error

4. Create destination file:
   create() / open(O_CREAT) → abort/truncate if exists

5. Copy Loop:
   read()  → from input file buffer
   write() → to destination file buffer
   repeat until read() returns 0 (EOF) or error

6. Clean up:
   close() input file
   close() destination file

7. Output status:
   write() → completion message

8. Termination:
   exit() → normal termination

items.title: System Call Categories (Windows vs Unix)
items.text: Category Windows API Unix/Linux Syscalls Process Control CreateProcess, ExitProcess, WaitForSingleObject fork, exec, wait, exit File Manipulation CreateFile, ReadFile, WriteFile, CloseHandle open, creat, read, write, close Device Manipulation SetConsoleMode, ReadConsole, WriteConsole ioctl, read, write Information Maintenance GetCurrentProcessId, SetTimer, Sleep getpid, alarm, sleep Communications CreatePipe, CreateFileMapping, MapViewOfFile pipe, shm_open, mmap Protection SetFileSecurity, InitializeSecurityDescriptor chmod, umask, chown

items.title: Standard C Library → System Call (printf → write)
items.text:
USER MODE:
main.c:      printf("Greetings\n");
                  │
                  ▼ Calls library function
libc:        Formats string buffer
             Invokes write() syscall stub
                  │ TRAP to Kernel (syscall instruction)
                  ▼
KERNEL MODE:
sys_write(): Executes, sends data to terminal
             Returns bytes written
                  │ Return from Trap
                  ▼
USER MODE:
libc write() stub passes control back to main()

items.title: Program vs Process
items.text:
Aspect Program Process Nature Passive (file on disk) Active (in execution) Context None PC, registers, memory space, stack Instances One file Multiple from same program

Silberschatz: "A program is a passive entity... A process is a program in execution."

items.title: Process Memory Layout (32-bit)
items.text:
High Address (0xFFFFFFFF)
├── Command-line args & Environment (argc, argv, envp)
├── STACK (grows ↓: frames, locals, params, return addresses)
│       ↑
│       │   (free space)
│       ↓
├── HEAP (grows ↑: malloc/free)
├── BSS (uninitialized globals/statics → zeroed)
├── DATA (initialized globals/statics)
└── TEXT (code, read-only)
Low Address (0x00000000)

items.title: C Mapping Example
items.text:
int x;              // → BSS (uninitialized)
int y = 15;         // → DATA (initialized)

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {  // args in high memory
    int *values;    // → STACK (pointer)
    int i;          // → STACK (local)
    values = malloc(5 * sizeof(int)); // → HEAP
    for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) values[i] = i;  // → TEXT executes
    return 0;
}

items.title: 3.4 Process State Model (5-State)
items.text:
[ NEW ]
                        │
                     admitted
                        ▼
         +────────> [ READY ] <─────────+
         │           │                   │
         │  dispatch │                   │
         │           ▼                   │
         │    [ RUNNING ] ──────────────+
         │        │        interrupt
         │        │
         │        │ I/O wait
         │        ▼
         │    [ WAITING ]
         │        │
         +────────┘
          I/O complete

   [ RUNNING ] ─────────> [ TERMINATED ]
             exit
State Meaning New Being created Ready In memory, waiting for CPU Running Executing on CPU Waiting Blocked on I/O/event Terminated Finished, awaiting cleanup

items.title: 3.5 Process Control Block (PCB / task_struct)
items.text:
Kernel representation of each process

PCB Field Description Process State Ready, Running, Waiting... Process ID (PID) Unique identifier Program Counter Next instruction address CPU Registers Accumulator, index, stack pointer Scheduling Info Priority, queue pointers Memory Management Page tables, base/limit Accounting CPU time used, time limits I/O Status Allocated devices, open files

Linux task_struct: pid, state, mm (memory), files (fd table), parent, children

items.title: Three Queues
items.text: Queue Contents Job Queue All processes in system Ready Queue In memory, ready to execute Device/Waiting Queues Blocked on specific I/O/event

items.title: Scheduler Types
items.text: Scheduler Frequency Role Short-term (CPU) Milliseconds Pick next ready process → dispatch Long-term (Job) Seconds/minutes Admit from disk to memory (controls degree of multiprogramming) Medium-term (Swapper) As needed Swap out to disk (free memory) → swap in later

items.title: Process Types
items.text:
Type Behavior CPU Bursts I/O-Bound More I/O than compute Many, short CPU-Bound More compute than I/O Few, long

Scheduler goal: Balance mix for good utilization + responsiveness

items.title: 3.7 Context Switching
items.text:
Mechanism: Save current process state to PCB, load next process state from PCB

P0 Running → Interrupt → Save PCB0 → Load PCB1 → P1 Running
             ↑                               │
             └── Interrupt → Save PCB1 → Load PCB0 ───┘

items.title: Overhead (Pure System Cost)
items.text:
• Save/restore: GPRs, PC, SP, FP registers
  • Flush/invalidate TLB
  • Switch address space (page table base register)
  • Factors: Hardware register sets, PCB size, OS complexity

Silberschatz: "Context-switch time is pure overhead, because the system does no useful work while switching."

items.title: 3.8 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. OS Services: User-facing (UI, exec, I/O, files, comm, errors) + System-facing (resource allocation, accounting, protection)
  2. System Calls: API to kernel; categories: process, file, device, info, comm, protection
  3. Process = active entity with memory layout (TEXT, DATA, BSS, HEAP, STACK)
  4. 5-State Model: New → Ready ↔ Running → Waiting → Terminated
  5. PCB = kernel's process representation (Linux: task_struct)
  6. Three Schedulers: Short-term (CPU), Long-term (admission), Medium-term (swapping)
  7. Context Switch = save/restore PCB + TLB flush + address space switch

items.title: 3.9 Quick Self-Test
items.text: Question Answer What are the 3 scheduler types? Short-term (CPU), Long-term (Job), Medium-term (Swapper) What does long-term scheduler control? Degree of multiprogramming What's in the PCB? State, PID, PC, registers, scheduling info, memory mgmt, accounting, I/O status Difference: I/O-bound vs CPU-bound? I/O-bound: many short bursts; CPU-bound: few long bursts Context switch overhead includes? Save/restore registers, TLB flush, page table switch printf → write syscall path? User: printf → libc formats → write stub → TRAP → Kernel: sys_write → returns

items.title: Topic 4: Process Creation, Termination & System Calls
items.text: Source: Lecture 5 + Textbook Ch. 3 (Silberschatz §3.4-3.5, Stevens & Rago Ch. 8)

items.title: The Unix Way
items.text:
pid = fork();  // Clone current process!
if (pid == 0) {
    // CHILD: Different program entirely
    exec("/bin/ls", "ls", NULL);  // Replaces memory with new program
} else {
    // PARENT: Continues original program
    wait(NULL);  // Wait for child to finish
}

Stevens & Rago: "The fork() function is the only way a new process is created by an existing process."

items.title: Why This Design?
items.text:
• fork() copies everything (with Copy-on-Write optimization)
  • exec() loads new program
  • Separation allows: setup pipes, change directories, drop privileges before loading new program

items.title: fork() Semantics
items.text: Context Return Child 0 Parent Child's PID (>0) Error -1

items.title: Copy-on-Write (COW)
items.text:
• Parent and child share physical pages read-only initially
  • When either writes → page is duplicated (page fault → kernel copies page)
  • Makes fork() fast; exec() discards COW pages anyway

items.title: 4.2 Complete fork() + exec() + wait() Program
items.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int main() {
    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Fork Failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    else if (pid == 0) {
        // CHILD: Execute new program
        execlp("/bin/ls", "ls", NULL);
    }
    else {
        // PARENT: Wait for child
        wait(NULL);
        printf("Child Complete\n");
    }
    return 0;
}

items.title: 4.3 exec() Family
items.text:
Function Arguments Environment PATH Search execl(path, arg0, ..., NULL) List Inherited No execv(path, argv[]) Vector Inherited No execle(path, arg0, ..., NULL, envp[]) List Custom No execve(path, argv[], envp[]) Vector Custom TRUE SYSCALL execlp(file, arg0, ..., NULL) List Inherited Yes execvp(file, argv[]) Vector Inherited Yes fexecve(fd, argv[], envp[]) Vector Custom From fd

Mnemonic: l=list, v=vector, p=PATH search, e=environment, f=file descriptor

items.title: Normal Termination (5 ways)
items.text:
1. return from main()
  2. exit() — flushes buffers, runs atexit handlers
  3. _exit() / _Exit() — direct kernel call, no cleanup
  4. Last thread returns from start routine
  5. pthread_exit() from last thread

items.title: Abnormal Termination (3 ways)
items.text:
1. abort() → SIGABRT
  2. Signals: SIGKILL, SIGSEGV, SIGFPE
  3. Last thread responds to cancellation

items.title: 4.4 Zombie vs Orphan Processes
items.text:
Zombie Orphan Cause Child exited, parent hasn't wait() Parent exited before child State Dead but PID+status in process table Alive, no parent Resolution Parent calls wait() → reaped Re-parented to init/systemd (PID 1) In ps <defunct> Normal process

Stevens & Rago: "A process that has terminated, but whose parent has not yet waited for it, is called a zombie."

items.title: 4.5 wait() & waitpid()
items.text:
#include <sys/wait.h>

pid_t wait(int *statloc);           // Blocks until ANY child terminates
pid_t waitpid(pid_t pid, int *statloc, int options);
pid value Meaning > 0 Wait for specific child PID -1 Wait for any child (like wait()) 0 Wait for any child in same process group < -1 Wait for any child in process group \|pid\|

Options: WNOHANG = non-blocking (returns 0 if no child terminated)

items.title: Extracting Exit Status
items.text:

int child_code = WEXITSTATUS(status);  // Gets 0-255 from child's exit()

items.title: 4.6 Race Conditions Post-fork()
items.text:
// After fork(), parent and child run CONCURRENTLY
// NEVER assume which runs first!

// FLAWED POLLING (never do this):
while (getppid() != 1) {  // Wait for reparenting to init
    sleep(1);  // Wastes CPU, induces latency
}

items.title: 4.7 I/O Request Life Cycle (I/O-Bound Process)
items.text:
1. Running: Process executes until I/O syscall (read/write)
2. Blocked: OS moves process to Waiting/Blocked queue
3. Preemption: CPU reassigned to another ready process
4. Device Servicing: Controller transfers data asynchronously
5. Interrupt: Device signals completion via hardware interrupt
6. Ready: OS moves process from Waiting → Ready queue
7. Resume: Scheduler dispatches process back to CPU

items.title: 4.8 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. fork() = creates child (COW), returns 0 to child, PID to parent, -1 on error
  2. exec() = replaces process image with new program; never returns on success
  3. wait()/waitpid() = reap zombies, get exit status via WEXITSTATUS
  4. Zombie = child dead, parent hasn't waited; Orphan = parent dead, child reparented to init
  5. COW = pages shared read-only until write → then duplicated
  6. Never assume parent/child execution order post-fork()
  7. Normal exit: return/exit()/_exit(); Abnormal: signals/abort()

Re-parented to init/systemd (PID 1) WEXITSTATUS(status) extracts? 8-bit exit code (0-255) from child COW = ? Copy-on-Write: share pages read-only until write _exit() vs exit()? _exit() = no cleanup, direct kernel call

items.title: Topic 5: CPU Scheduling — FCFS & SJF
items.text: Source: Lecture 7 + Textbook Ch. 4 (Silberschatz Ch. 5, Stallings Ch. 9, Stevens & Rago Ch. 9)

items.title: Why Scheduling?
items.text:
• Single CPU core → only one process executes at a time
  • Others wait in ready queue
  • Goal: Keep CPU busy at all times (maximize utilization)
  • When process waits for I/O → scheduler switches to another ready process

items.title: CPU-I/O Burst Cycle
items.text:
CPU burst → I/O burst → CPU burst → I/O burst → ...
- CPU burst distribution drives scheduling algorithm design - I/O-bound: many short CPU bursts - CPU-bound: few long CPU bursts

items.title: 5.2 Scheduler & Dispatcher
items.text: Component Role Short-term scheduler Picks next process from ready queue Dispatcher Context switch, mode change, jump to user code Dispatch latency Time to stop one process, start another

items.title: Four Decision Points
items.text: # Transition Non-Preemptive Preemptive 1 Running → Waiting (I/O) ✅ ✅ 2 Running → Ready (interrupt) ❌ ✅ 3 Waiting → Ready (I/O done) ❌ ✅ 4 Running → Terminated ✅ ✅ Type Description Non-Preemptive Process keeps CPU until it voluntarily releases (I/O or terminate) Preemptive OS can forcibly preempt on timer interrupt or higher-priority arrival

items.title: 5.4 Scheduling Criteria (Metrics)
items.text: Metric Formula Goal Turnaround Time (TAT) Completion - Arrival Minimize Waiting Time (WT) TAT - Burst = Completion - Arrival - Burst Minimize Response Time (RT) First Start - Arrival Minimize CPU Utilization % time CPU busy Maximize Throughput Processes completed / time Maximize

items.title: 5.5 First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
items.text:
• Algorithm: FIFO ready queue, non-preemptive
  • Simple but suffers Convoy Effect

items.title: Example 1: P1(24), P2(3), P3(3) at t=0
Example 2: P2(3), P3(3), P1(24) at t=0
Convoy Effect
items.text: Short I/O-bound processes stuck behind long CPU-bound process → poor CPU & device utilization.

items.title: 5.6 Shortest-Job-First (SJF) — Non-Preemptive
items.text:
• Algorithm: Pick process with smallest next CPU burst
  • Tie-breaker: FCFS
  • Provably optimal for minimum average waiting time (stationary processes)

items.title: Example: All arrive at t=0
items.text:
Process Burst P1 6 P2 8 P3 7 P4 3

Order: P4(3) → P1(6) → P3(7) → P2(8) 

Gantt: | P4 | P1 | P3 | P2 |
       0    3    9   16   24

Wait: P4=0, P1=3, P3=9, P2=16 → Avg = 7.0
vs FCFS (P1,P2,P3,P4): Avg = 10.25

items.title: 5.7 Shortest-Remaining-Time-First (SRTF) — Preemptive SJF
items.text: • Preempt if new arrival has shorter remaining burst than current

items.title: Example with Arrival Times
items.text:
Process Arrival Burst P1 0 8 P2 1 4 P3 2 9 P4 3 5

Timeline: 

t=0: P1 starts (rem=8)
t=1: P2 arrives (4 < 7) → preempt P1, run P2
t=2: P3 arrives (9 > 3) → P2 continues
t=3: P4 arrives (5 > 2) → P2 continues
t=5: P2 done. Ready: P1(7), P3(9), P4(5) → run P4
t=10: P4 done. Ready: P1(7), P3(9) → run P1
t=17: P1 done. Run P3
t=26: P3 done.

Gantt: | P1 | P2 | P4 | P1 | P3 |
       0    1    5   10   17   26

Waiting Times: | Process | Completion | Arrival | Burst | WT = CT - AT - BT | |---------|------------|---------|-------|-------------------| | P1 | 17 | 0 | 8 | 9 | | P2 | 5 | 1 | 4 | 0 | | P3 | 26 | 2 | 9 | 15 | | P4 | 10 | 3 | 5 | 2 | | Avg | | | | 6.5 |

items.text: Metric Formula Turnaround Time Completion - Arrival Waiting Time Turnaround - Burst = Completion - Arrival - Burst Response Time First Start - Arrival Avg Waiting Σ Wait_i / n RR Max Wait Bound (n - 1) × q

items.title: Topic 6: CPU Scheduling — Priority & Round Robin
items.text: Source: Lecture 8 + Textbook Ch. 4 (Silberschatz Ch. 5, Stallings Ch. 9)

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Each process has an integer priority
  • CPU → highest priority process
  • Conventions:
  • Silberschatz: Smaller integer = Higher priority (1 = highest)
  • Some systems: Larger integer = Higher priority
  • Always verify convention in problem

items.title: Modes
items.text: Mode Behavior Non-Preemptive Once CPU given, runs to completion (or I/O) Preemptive New arrival with higher priority preempts current

items.title: Relationship with SJF
items.text: • SJF = special case of Priority where priority = 1 / predicted burst time

items.title: Major Problem: Starvation
items.text:
• Low-priority process waits indefinitely if high-priority stream continues
  • Real case: MIT's IBM 7094 (1973) — low-priority job from 1967 still waiting!

items.title: Solution: Aging
items.text:
• Gradually increase priority of waiting processes (e.g., +1 every 15 min)
  • Eventually gets high enough priority to execute

items.title: Example 1: Non-Preemptive (Smaller = Higher Priority)
items.text:
Process Burst Priority P1 10 3 P2 1 1 (Highest) P3 2 4 P4 1 5 (Lowest) P5 5 2

Order: P2 → P5 → P1 → P3 → P4 

Gantt: | P2 | P5 | P1 | P3 | P4 |
       0    1    6   16   18   19

Wait: P1=6, P2=0, P3=16, P4=18, P5=1 → Avg = 8.2

items.title: Example 2: Preemptive (Larger = Higher Priority)
items.text:
Process Arrival Burst Priority P1 0 4 2 P2 1 3 3 P3 2 1 4 P4 3 5 5 (Highest) P5 4 2 5 (Highest)

Timeline: 

t=0: P1 starts (pri 2)
t=1: P2 arrives (pri 3 > 2) → preempt P1, run P2
t=2: P3 arrives (pri 4 > 3) → preempt P2, run P3
t=3: P3 done. P4 arrives (pri 5) → run P4
t=4: P5 arrives (pri 5 = P4) → FCFS keeps P4
t=8: P4 done. P5 (pri 5) runs 8-10
t=10: P5 done. Ready: P2(pri 3, rem 2), P1(pri 2, rem 3) → P2 runs 10-12
t=12: P2 done. P1 runs 12-15
t=15: P1 done.

Gantt: | P1 | P2 | P3 | P4 | P5 | P2 | P1 |
       0    1    2    3    8   10   12   15

Waiting Times: | Process | CT | AT | BT | WT = CT - AT - BT | |---------|-----|-----|-----|-------------------| | P1 | 15 | 0 | 4 | 11 | | P2 | 12 | 1 | 3 | 8 | | P3 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 | | P4 | 8 | 3 | 5 | 0 | | P5 | 10 | 4 | 2 | 4 | | Avg | | | | 4.6 |

items.title: Principles
items.text:
• Preemptive, based on FCFS
  • Time Quantum (q): 10-100ms typical
  • Ready queue = circular FIFO
  • Process runs ≤ q; if not done → preempted → appended to tail

items.title: Example: q=4, P1(24), P2(3), P3(3) at t=0
items.text:
t=0:  P1 runs 4ms (rem=20) → tail
t=4:  P2 runs 3ms (done) → terminates at 7
t=7:  P3 runs 3ms (done) → terminates at 10
t=10: Only P1 remains → runs in 4ms quanta until done at 30

Gantt: | P1 | P2 | P3 | P1 | P1 | P1 | P1 | P1 |
       0    4    7   10   14   18   22   26   30

Waiting Times: - P1: Runs [0-4], waits [4-10], runs to finish → Wait = 6 - P2: Waits [0-4] → Wait = 4 - P3: Waits [0-7] → Wait = 7 - Avg WT = 5.66

items.title: Time Quantum Trade-offs
items.text: Quantum Size Behavior q → ∞ Degenerates to FCFS q → 0 Approaches processor sharing (each gets 1/n speed) but context-switch overhead dominates

items.title: Maximum Waiting Bound
items.text:
If n processes in ready queue, time quantum = q:
No process waits longer than (n - 1) × q time units

items.title: Rule of Thumb (Silberschatz)
items.text: ~80% of CPU bursts should complete within one quantum

items.title: 6.5 Quick Comparison Table
items.text: Algorithm Preemptive? Starvation? Best For FCFS No No Simple batch SJF No Yes (long jobs) Minimum wait SRTF Yes Yes (long jobs) Responsive batch Priority Both Yes (fix: aging) Importance-based RR Yes No Time-sharing MLFQ Yes No (with aging) General purpose

Aging (gradually boost waiting process priority) RR quantum → ∞? Becomes FCFS RR quantum → 0? Processor sharing but context-switch overhead kills performance RR max wait bound? (n - 1) × q RR quantum guideline? 80% of bursts complete within one quantum

items.text:

  • Q29: 80% rule for quantum selection
  • Q30: Priority inversion — high blocked on low, medium runs → fix: Priority Inheritance

items.title: Topic 7: CPU Scheduling — Multilevel Queue & Multilevel Feedback Queue
items.text: Source: Lecture 10 + Textbook Ch. 4 (Silberschatz Ch. 5)

items.title: Motivation
items.text:
• Processes can be classified into distinct groups with different response-time requirements
  • Single ready queue is inadequate

items.title: Common Partitioning
items.text: Queue Type Processes Scheduling Foreground Interactive (low response time) Round-Robin Background Batch jobs (throughput priority) FCFS

items.title: Permanent Assignment
items.text:
• Processes permanently assigned to one queue at creation
  • Based on: memory size, process priority, process type

items.title: Inter-Queue Scheduling Policies
items.text: Policy Behavior Fixed-Priority Preemptive Higher queues must empty first; lower queues starve if higher busy Time-Sliced Each queue gets CPU fraction (e.g., 80% foreground, 20% background)

items.title: Core Innovation
items.text:
• Unlike MLQ, processes migrate between queues dynamically
  • Adapts to runtime CPU-burst characteristics
  • Implements Aging to prevent starvation

items.title: Defining Parameters (5)
items.text:
1. Number of queues
  2. Scheduling algorithm per queue
  3. Promotion (upgrade) method
  4. Demotion (downgrade) method
  5. Initial queue for new processes

items.title: Execution & Demotion Rules
items.text:
1. Q0 (RR, q=8): New process enters; if uses full 8ms → demoted to Q1
  2. Q1 (RR, q=16): Runs only when Q0 empty; if uses full 16ms → demoted to Q2
  3. Q2 (FCFS): Runs only when Q0 & Q1 empty
  4. Preemption: Q0 arrival preempts Q1/Q2; Q1 arrival preempts Q2

items.title: Promotion (Aging) Policy
items.text:
• If process waits too long in Q2 without CPU → promoted to Q1 or Q0
  • Guarantees long-running jobs eventually make progress

items.title: 7.3 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. MLQ: Fixed queues, no migration → starvation risk in lower queues
  2. MLFQ: Dynamic migration → learns process behavior (I/O-bound stay high, CPU-bound sink low)
  3. Aging: Prevents starvation by promoting long-waiting processes
  4. Modern OS: Linux CFS, Windows, macOS use MLFQ variants

items.title: 7.4 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q31: MLQ rigidity — processes permanently assigned, cannot migrate
  • Q32: MLFQ demotion — CPU-bound processes use full quantum → demoted; I/O-bound release early → stay high

items.title: Topic 8: Shell Programming & Cron Scheduling
items.text: Source: Lecture 11 + Textbook Ch. 10 (Stevens & Rago Ch. 9-10)

items.title: Definition & Role
items.text:
[ User / Terminal ] ↔ [ Shell Interpreter ] ↔ [ OS Kernel ] ↔ [ Hardware ]
- Command-line interpreter (CLI) — reads commands, parses, resolves executables, requests kernel to spawn processes - Also a programming language (variables, conditionals, loops, functions)

items.title: Command Syntax & Parsing
items.text:
command [options] [arguments]
- Tokenizes into: command name, flags/options, target arguments - Path resolution: - Absolute/relative path (./script, /bin/ls) → direct access - Name only (ls) → searches $PATH directories left-to-right

items.text:
Shell Origin Notes sh Stephen Bourne, AT&T Bell Labs Original Bourne shell csh/tcsh Bill Joy, UC Berkeley C-like syntax ksh David Korn Combines Bourne + C shell features bash GNU Project Default on modern Linux 
echo $SHELL  # Shows active login shell

items.text:
Statement Effect continue Skip rest of current iteration → next iteration break Exit loop entirely → statement after loop

items.text:

items.text:
#include <stdio.h>
FILE *popen(const char *cmdstring, const char *type);  // type: "r" or "w"

items.title: Topic 9: Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing
items.text: Source: Lecture 1 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 5 (Silberschatz Ch. 3, Stallings Ch. 5, 17, Stevens & Rago Ch. 14-15, 17)

items.title: Process Types
items.text: Type Description Independent Cannot affect/be affected by others; shares no data Cooperating Can affect/be affected; shares data, memory, messages

items.title: Reasons for Cooperation
items.text:
1. Information Sharing — Concurrent access to shared resources (files, DBs)
  2. Computation Speedup — Parallel subtasks across CPU cores
  3. Modularity — Divide OS/apps into cooperating processes (client-server, microservices)
  4. Convenience — User running concurrent tasks

items.title: 9.2 Two Fundamental Models
items.text: Aspect Shared Memory Message Passing Mechanism OS maps shared region into both address spaces send()/receive() via kernel Speed Fastest (memory speed, no kernel copies) Slower (user→kernel→user copies) Sync Manual (semaphores, mutexes) Built into send/receive Best For Large data, same machine Distributed systems, small data

items.title: Architectural Comparison
items.text:
SHARED MEMORY                    MESSAGE PASSING
Process A    Process B            Process A    Process B
    │           │                    │           │
    ▼           ▼                    ▼           ▼
┌───────────────────────┐      ┌───────────────────────┐
│    SHARED MEMORY      │      │       OS KERNEL       │
│    [ Data Buffer ]    │      │  [M1] [M2] [M3] Queue │
└───────────────────────┘      └───────────────────────┘

items.title: Characteristics
items.text:
• OS establishes shared region mapped into both address spaces
  • Subsequent reads/writes at memory speed in user mode — no OS intervention
  • Fastest IPC

items.title: Challenges
items.text:
• Synchronization — If writer writes while reader reads → corruption
  • Must use: POSIX Semaphores, Mutex Locks, File/Record Locking

items.title: Linux Memory Layout with Shared Memory
Core Primitives
items.text:
• send(message) — blocks or returns immediately
  • receive(message) — blocks or returns immediately

items.title: Communication Link Design Questions
items.text:
1. How are links established?
  2. Can a link connect >2 processes?
  3. How many links between a pair?
  4. What is message capacity?
  5. Fixed or variable message size?
  6. Unidirectional or bidirectional?

items.title: 9.5 Direct Communication
items.text:
send(P, message);        // Send directly to process P
receive(Q, &message);    // Receive directly from process Q
Property Behavior Naming Explicit (PID) Link Auto-established between pair Multiplicity One link per pair Direction Usually bidirectional

Disadvantage: Hardcoded PIDs → fragile; changing PID requires updating all references

items.title: 9.6 Indirect Communication (Mailboxes / Ports)
items.text:
send(A, message);        // Send to mailbox A
receive(A, &message);    // Receive from mailbox A
Property Behavior Naming Via mailbox/port ID Link Exists only if processes share mailbox Multiplicity Many processes can share mailbox; pair can share multiple mailboxes Direction Unidirectional or bidirectional

items.title: Multi-Receiver Ambiguity
items.text:
P1 → Mailbox A ← P2
              ← P3
If P1 sends, both P2 and P3 receive() → who gets it?

Solutions: 1. Restrict mailbox to ≤2 processes 2. Mutex on receive() (only one receiver at a time) 3. OS arbitrates, notifies sender of chosen recipient

items.title: 9.7 Synchronization Modes
items.text: Mode Send Behavior Receive Behavior Blocking (Synchronous) Blocks until message received Blocks until message available Non-blocking (Async) Returns immediately Returns message or null immediately

items.title: Rendezvous
items.text:
• Both send and receive are blocking
  • Sender and receiver synchronize tightly at exchange moment

items.title: 9.8 Buffering Capacities
items.text: Capacity Behavior Zero (No Buffer) Sender blocks until receiver ready (strict rendezvous) Bounded (n messages) Sender blocks only when queue full Unbounded Sender never blocks; risk of memory exhaustion

items.title: Bounded Buffer (Circular Array)
items.text:
#define BUFFER_SIZE 10
item buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
int in = 0;   // Next free slot
int out = 0;  // First full slot

// Empty: in == out
// Full:  (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE == out
// Usable capacity: BUFFER_SIZE - 1

items.title: Naive Code (Busy Waiting = Bad)
items.text:
// Producer
while (true) {
    produce(item);
    while (((in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE) == out); // SPIN
    buffer[in] = item;
    in = (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
}

// Consumer
while (true) {
    while (in == out); // SPIN
    item = buffer[out];
    out = (out + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
    consume(item);
}
Problem: Busy waiting burns CPU — use blocking semaphores instead!

items.title: Pipes (Anonymous) — pipe()
items.text:
int fd[2];
pipe(fd);  // fd[0]=read, fd[1]=write
- Half-duplex (unidirectional) - Ancestry required — only parent/child (must pipe() before fork())

items.title: FIFOs (Named Pipes) — mkfifo()
items.text:
mkfifo("/tmp/myfifo", 0666);
- Exists in filesystem (type p) - Unrelated processes can communicate - Open with open(), use read()/write()/close()

items.title: System V Message Queues
items.text:
struct msgbuf { long mtype; char mtext[...]; };
msgget(key, flags);     // Create/get queue
msgsnd(msqid, &msg, ...); // Send
msgrcv(msqid, &msg, ..., type); // Receive with TYPE FILTERING
- Key feature: msgrcv() can selectively fetch by mtype (priority)

items.title: System V Semaphores
items.text:
semget(key, nsems, flags);
semctl(semid, semnum, cmd, ...);
semop(semid, sembuf_array, nops); // ATOMIC multiple operations

items.title: Unix Domain Sockets (AF_UNIX)
items.text:
• Bidirectional, full socket API, no network overhead
  • Supports file descriptor passing (SCM_RIGHTS)
  • Used by: systemd, Docker, X11/Wayland, PostgreSQL

items.title: 9.11 Modern IPC (What You Actually Use)
items.text: Instead of Raw... Use... shmget + mutex Redis, memcached, SQLite WAL, mmap'ed files msgget/msgsnd RabbitMQ, Kafka, ZeroMQ, gRPC, D-Bus Pipes Shell pipelines cmd1 \| cmd2 Sockets systemd, Docker, databases

items.title: 9.12 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• IPC = controlled isolation breaking for cooperation [Silberschatz §3.1]
  • Shared memory = speed + manual sync (whiteboard model) [Silberschatz §3.3]
  • Message passing = safety + built-in sync + distribution (postal model) [Silberschatz §3.4]
  • Producer-consumer = fundamental pattern [Silberschatz §3.5]
  • Busy waiting = bad in user space — use blocking primitives [Silberschatz §3.5.2]
  • Bounded buffers give backpressure for free
  • Mailboxes decouple sender/receiver → modularity [Silberschatz §3.4.4]

items.title: 9.13 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q46: Shared memory fastest — zero kernel copy after setup
  • Q47: Message passing — each send/receive = kernel syscall, slower but simpler for distributed
  • Q48: Socket endpoint = IP address + Port number
  • Q43: Pipe descriptors — parent closes fd[0] (read), child closes fd[1] (write)

items.title: Topic 10: Threads & Multicore Programming
items.text: Source: Lecture 2 & 4 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 6 (Silberschatz Ch. 4, Stallings Ch. 4, Stevens & Rago Ch. 11-12)

items.title: Thread vs Process
items.text:
Aspect Process Thread Memory Isolated address space Shared (code, data, heap, files) Private PID, address space, FD table TID, PC, registers, stack, errno Creation cost High (~30× thread) Low Context switch Slow (~5× thread) Fast Protection Strong (fault isolates) None (bug crashes all)

Silberschatz: "A thread is a basic unit of CPU utilization; it comprises a thread ID, a program counter, a register set, and a stack."

items.title: Thread Structure
items.text: Thread = (TID, Program Counter, Register Set, Private Stack)

items.title: Process Architecture
items.text:
SINGLE-THREADED                    MULTITHREADED
┌─────────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────────┐
│ Code | Data | Files │           │ Code | Data | Files │  ← SHARED
├─────────────────────┤           ├─────────────────────┤
│ Registers | Stack   │           │ Regs | Regs | Regs  │
│             │       │           │ Stack|Stack|Stack  │  ← PER-THREAD
└─────────────────────┘           └─────────────────────┘

items.title: 10.2 Benefits of Multithreading
items.text: Benefit Description Responsiveness UI stays responsive while background thread computes Resource Sharing Threads share memory/files automatically — no IPC needed Economy Thread create ≈ 30× faster than process; context switch ≈ 5× faster Scalability Threads run on multiple cores simultaneously

items.title: Real-World Examples
items.text:
• Web Browser: Network thread, render thread, audio thread, UI thread
  • Word Processor: Input thread, spell-check thread, autosave thread

items.title: 10.3 Multithreading Models
items.text:
Model User:Kernel Parallelism Blocking Issue Used By Many-to-One (M:1) Many:1 ❌ No One blocks → all block Old Solaris, Green threads One-to-One (1:1) 1:1 ✅ Yes No blocking propagation Linux, Windows, macOS Many-to-Many (M:N) Many:Many ✅ Yes Flexible multiplexing Old Solaris Two-Level (Hybrid) Hybrid ✅ Yes Critical threads bound 1:1 IRIX, HP-UX, Solaris 8- 
1:1 Model (Modern Standard):
User:  T1  T2  T3  T4
        │  │  │  │
Kernel: KT1 KT2 KT3 KT4

Silberschatz: "The one-to-one model is the most common model used in modern operating systems."

items.title: Thread Creation
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>

int pthread_create(
    pthread_t *thread,           // OUT: thread ID
    const pthread_attr_t *attr,  // Attributes (NULL = defaults)
    void *(*start_routine)(void *), // Function pointer
    void *arg                    // Single argument (void*)
);

// Thread function signature:
void *my_thread_func(void *arg) {
    // do work
    return NULL;  // or pthread_exit(retval)
}

Stevens & Rago: "The pthread_create() function creates a new thread of control that executes concurrently with the calling thread."

items.title: Critical: Stack-Escape Bug
items.text:
// ❌ WRONG - passes address of LOCAL variable
void start_thread(int value) {
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, &value); // DANGER!
    // if start_thread() returns before worker runs...
    // value is gone! Stack frame destroyed!
}

// ✅ CORRECT - allocate on heap
void start_thread(int value) {
    int *arg = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *arg = value;
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, arg);
    // worker must free(arg) when done
}

// ✅ CORRECT - pass from main() stack (main never returns)
int main() {
    int value = 42;  // lives until program ends
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, &value);
    pthread_join(tid, NULL);
}

Rule: Argument pointer must remain valid until thread finishes using it.

items.title: Thread Join — Synchronization & Cleanup
items.text:
int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);
// Blocks until 'thread' terminates
// retval receives return value

Why join? 1. Wait for result — main needs worker's output 2. Prevent zombie threads — unjoined threads leak resources (TCB, stack) 3. Orderly shutdown — ensure workers done before exit

// Fork-Join Pattern [Silberschatz Fig. 4.3]
pthread_t threads[N];
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, worker, &args[i]);

for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    pthread_join(threads[i], &results[i]);  // Collect results

items.title: pthread_exit() vs exit() vs return in main()
items.text: Call Effect pthread_exit(val) Current thread only dies; process lives if other threads exist return val in thread func Same as pthread_exit(val) exit(val) or return in main() Entire process dies — all threads killed instantly pthread_exit() in main() Main thread dies, other threads keep running

items.title: Scheduling Scopes
Mutex (Mutual Exclusion Lock)
items.text:
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);   // Blocks if busy
// CRITICAL SECTION
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock); // Must be called by owner

items.title: Condition Variables (Wait for Predicate)
items.text:
pthread_cond_t cond = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
pthread_mutex_t mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

// Waiter
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
while (!condition) pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex);
// Condition is true, mutex held
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

// Signaler
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
condition = true;
pthread_cond_signal(&cond);  // or broadcast
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

items.title: 10.6 Thread Cancellation
10.7 Thread Pools
items.text:
Problem: Creating/destroying threads per request = overhead + unbounded resource use

Architecture: 

// Startup: create fixed pool
for (i = 0; i < POOL_SIZE; i++)
    pthread_create(&pool[i], NULL, worker_loop, &queue);

// Worker loop
void *worker_loop(void *arg) {
    while (true) {
        Task *t = queue_pop(&queue);  // Blocks if empty
        execute(t);
        // Thread returns to pool, doesn't die
    }
}

// Submit work
queue_push(&queue, new_task);  // Wakes one worker

Used everywhere: nginx, Apache, Java ExecutorService, C++ std::thread_pool

Silberschatz: "A thread pool provides a more efficient way to manage threads... it reduces the overhead of creating and destroying threads."

items.title: 10.8 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• Thread = lightweight execution unit sharing process resources [Silberschatz §4.1]
  • 1:1 model = modern standard (Linux, Windows, macOS) [Silberschatz §4.3.2]
  • Pthreads = POSIX standard; pthread_create, join, exit, mutex, cond [Stevens & Rago Ch. 11]
  • Stack-escape bug = never pass local stack address to new thread [Stevens & Rago §11.3]
  • Join prevents zombies = always join non-detached threads [Stevens & Rago §11.4]
  • Shared vs Private = globals/heap shared; stack/registers/PC private [Silberschatz §4.2]
  • SCS (System scope) = Linux default; threads compete globally [Silberschatz §4.4.2]
  • Thread pools = reuse threads, bound resources, lower latency [Silberschatz §4.5]
  • Deferred cancellation = safe; async cancellation = dangerous [Stevens & Rago §11.8]
